messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

John, a 55-year-old North American male and fashion designer, has been struggling with a complex interplay of symptoms stemming from childhood physical abuse by his caregiver. His current state is marked by a pervasive sense of vulnerability and mistrust, as well as a deep-seated fear that he will never recover from the trauma he experienced. Growing up in a small Midwestern town, John endured years of brutal beatings at the hands of his father. The abuse was not only physical but also psychological, leaving him with a fragmented memory of the events and an overwhelming sense of guilt. Even now, decades later, John cannot piece together a coherent narrative of what happened to him. When he does recall specific instances of abuse, he feels as if they occurred to someone else—emotionless and detached from his own experience. The trauma has left deep scars on John’s psyche. He often ruminates about the actions of others that have wronged him, particularly focusing on how he was victimized by his father. This rumination is accompanied by a relentless self-blame where he questions what he could have done differently to prevent the abuse. These thoughts are compounded by intense nightmares that occur at specific times of day or in certain situations, making it difficult for John to sleep without fear. John’s heightened state of alertness is evident in his daily life. He reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly, a reaction rooted in the unpredictable nature of the beatings he experienced as a child. The absence of sound in his home environment can also trigger a sense of impending danger, making it challenging for John to relax even within the safety of his own house. John’s occupation as a fashion designer has not been spared by these symptoms. His constant state of alertness often makes it difficult for him to collaborate effectively with colleagues who frequently touch or pat him on the back in a show of camaraderie, actions that trigger his fight-or-flight response. This hyper-vigilance has led to strained relationships at work and a perception among his peers that he is aloof or disengaged. Over time, John’s avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on his personal life as well. His fear of being touched by others has made it difficult for him to maintain close relationships, further isolating him from potential sources of support. The mistrust he harbors towards people stems from the belief that no one can be truly relied upon—a sentiment deeply ingrained by his childhood experiences. John’s self-doubt is profound; he believes he will never fully recover from the trauma and fears that his current reactions mean he is “going crazy.” These negative appraisals have created a vicious cycle where John feels permanently damaged, unable to escape the shadow of his past. His inability to form a coherent narrative about what happened has only reinforced this belief. Despite his efforts to cope with these overwhelming feelings, John’s quality of life has significantly deteriorated. The cumulative impact of his symptoms led him to finally seek help when he realized that his work and personal relationships were being severely affected. He is most afraid of the possibility of never regaining a sense of normalcy or stability. However, amidst this struggle, John also holds hope for a better future. He is eager to explore ways in which he can process his trauma more effectively and regain control over his life. His journey towards healing will involve understanding and making sense of his fragmented memories, addressing his intense feelings of guilt and mistrust, and finding healthier coping mechanisms that do not isolate him further from the world around him. John’s story is one of resilience in the face of profound adversity. Through therapy, he hopes to uncover a more coherent narrative of his past, regain trust in others, and ultimately reclaim a sense of control over his life.
